description: Usguri Dufutti are back (estão de volta, para os leigos do inglês)
summary:
Salus is a personal health console for astronauts on long missions, built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (“Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions”). On the way to Mars, the nearest doctor is millions of kilometers and minutes of delay away, so the crew member must be their own first responder. Salus gathers health indicators, compares them with the astronaut’s own baseline and suggests what to do, without waiting for Earth. Every screen answers three questions in seconds: am I OK, why, and what do I do now?

Indicators are organized around NASA’s five Human Research Program hazards: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile and closed environments. A readiness score with five hazard arcs surrounds an interactive 3D body. Salus handles a solar particle event (move to shelter, with NOAA space-weather context) and warns when hazards compound. It adapts to the mission profile (LEO, Moon, Mars) and offers a daily check-in, a watch glance, and views for the crew medical officer and the flight surgeon.

Every action is a suggestion with what to do, why, for how long, and its source, and nothing is worded as a diagnosis. The prototype runs offline in the browser, backed by a lightweight Python and SQLite server that stores the crew member’s state. All data is simulated.
details:
What it does. Salus is a health console for astronauts on long missions. It gathers health indicators (sleep, heart rate, blood oxygen, exercise, radiation dose and mood check-ins) and compares each one with the astronaut’s own baseline. It then tells them, in a few seconds, whether they are OK, why, and what to do now. Indicators are grouped under NASA’s five Human Research Program hazards, shown as five arcs of a readiness score around an interactive 3D body. Salus reacts to events such as a solar particle event, where it tells the astronaut to move to shelter, using NOAA space-weather context. It warns when several hazards add up, and it adapts to the mission profile (LEO, Moon, Mars). It also has a watch glance and views for the crew medical officer and the flight surgeon on Earth.

Benefits. The crew can act on their own health without waiting for Earth, which matters when the comm delay is several minutes. Every suggestion shows what to do, why, for how long, and its source. One screen replaces scattered readings.

Intended impact. Safer autonomy on deep-space missions, and the same loop on Earth for people far from care: remote workers, rural patients and older adults living alone.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with three.js for the 3D body. A backend in Python (standard library only) with a SQLite database and a JSON API, plus Docker. Data context comes from NASA HRP and NOAA SWPC. We used Claude Code to work faster and for extra reviews. No special hardware: the watch is simulated in the browser.

Creativity. The interface reads like flight instruments, not a hospital dashboard. Health is mapped onto NASA’s five hazards around a 3D body, and the screen tells the astronaut what to do instead of only showing numbers.

Factors we considered.

Comm delay and crew autonomy. The crew has to decide without Earth.

Glanceability under stress. Each screen answers its three questions in seconds.

Honesty. It is not a medical device, every screen is labeled as simulated data, every suggestion has a source, and nothing is worded as a diagnosis.

Accessibility. Status always appears as color, icon and word together; contrast meets WCAG AA; and it respects reduced-motion settings.

Offline use. Everything runs without internet.

Two audiences. The astronaut on board and the medical team on Earth.
